body:
Parker says he will "most likely" remain on the sideline, but the addition of Mike Pettine underscores the urgency in Dallas
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:28 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        FRISCO, Texas -- Any football fan knows that when a coach or coordinator is moved up to the booth, it's the start of a performance improvement plan that typically does not end well.Jerry Jones said Tuesday on 105.3 The Fan that Christian Parker would move upstairs for Week 6. Parker himself pushed back on that notion on Thursday, saying he will "most likely" remain down on the sideline. "There's advantages of both for sure, but I've always been a guy that's usually been down on the field," Parker said. Parker also received the dreaded vote of confidence from Brian Schottenheimer amid his struggling defense's performance in the Cowboys' 2-3 start to the 2026 season. That came in the wake of Dallas hiring former Cleveland Browns coach Mike Pettine as a senior assistant. Pettine actually gave Parker his first job in the NFL when he was Green Bay's defensive coordinator in 2019.   
"Christian Parker is our defensive coordinator and everything, all decisions, will run through him," Schottenheimer said Wednesday. "We're supporting him. I support him. I believe so strongly in the guy. I do. I think the guy's an incredible football coach. We have to coach better. We got to play better. I think our players will be the first ones to say there's things that they need to do better. There's things I need to do better.  And so no one is sitting here pointing fingers at Christian Parker. But as the head coach, you have to make decisions that you think helps you win games. That's not just adding a Mike Pettine, it's some of the personnel adjustments that I know you guys are dying to know about that are being worked on behind the scenes and communicated to the players."Dallas knows that being the league's 31st-ranked total defense (395.4 total yards per game allowed), last-place run defense (168.4 rushing yards per game allowed) and worst third-down defense (52.6% third-down conversion rate allowed) won't cut it.How fixable are the issues? "Very fixable because they're under our control," Parker said. "Very fixable."The level of urgency Parker and his players have shown through five weeks is far from an overreaction. Matt Eberflus, Parker's predecessor in 2025, had the Dallas defense looking very similar through five weeks. The only significant difference is that Eberflus' unit was the league's worst against the pass, while Parker's is the league's worst against the run.

He and the team were ramping up for him to be a full-time starter after being on the roster for a week, but he was scratched shortly before kickoff in Week 5 because he couldn't stop throwing up. Losing his No. 1 corner that close to kickoff was something Parker called "not ideal." However, he and Porter Jr. are ready for him to have a "heavily increased" workload against the Green Bay Packers.Look for rookie first-round edge rusher Malachi Lawrence to get more involved. Lawrence racked up his first career sack as well as a pass defensed in Week 5 against the Buccaneers. His quarterback pressure rate of 14.3% ranks fourth among qualified rookies, according to Pro Football Focus. He trails only David Bailey (16.4%), Sonny Styles (15%) and Cashius Howell (14.8%). Through five weeks, Lawrence co-leads the Cowboys in sacks with 1.0 despite playing significantly fewer pass rush snaps than some of Dallas' other edge rushers and defensive linemen. "Played very well," Schottenheimer said. title: Jalen Hurts blood clot: What is a superficial blood clot and how long could Eagles' QB be out - CBS Sports
description: Movement in a blood clot detected in a follow-up ultrasound has sidelined Philadelphia's star indefinitely after
body:
Movement in a blood clot detected in a follow-up ultrasound has sidelined Philadelphia's star indefinitely after he initially played through the clot against the Jaguars
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:58 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Philadelphia Eagles were dealt quite a blow this week, as they revealed star quarterback Jalen Hurts was managing a superficial blood clot and would not play vs. the Carolina Panthers on Sunday. Given the situation, it wouldn't be surprising if Hurts missed more than one game.In their statement released on Thursday, the Eagles said that four days after the Week 4 loss to the Los Angeles Rams, Hurts requested treatment on his calf. He believed he was kicked or cleated in the game, and his leg was bothering him. The Eagles performed an ultrasound on their quarterback's leg after they landed in London last week, and that's when the superficial blood clot was discovered. However, the Eagles' medical staff determined Hurts could suit up against the Jacksonville Jaguars. On Wednesday, back in Philadelphia, the Eagles conducted a follow-up ultrasound, during which they saw that the clot had moved. That's notable. While the Eagles have not disclosed exact details of the situation, the movement of a blood clot could potentially lead to a pulmonary embolism, which could be very serious. Hurts told reporters on Wednesday that his "calf injury" was "a very unique experience, to say the least," and that he got "nicked up" in the Rams game. Now, he's dealing with a situation that will hold him out indefinitely. 
Let's take a look at what's going on with Hurts.What is a 'superficial blood clot?'The Eagles did not go into detail about the clot, but the fact that it's "superficial" is likely a good sign. This could be classified as "superficial thrombophlebitis," per Harvard Health Publishing. An article found on The Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) describes a condition called "superficial vein thrombosis" (SuVT), where clots develop in superficial veins, typically in the legs or arms. Superficial veins are those closer to the surface of the skin. Risk factors include varicose veins, recent trauma, immobility and surgery. This is different than "deep vein thrombosis," which is a much more serious condition that requires anti-clotting drugs, and could have completely ended Hurts' 2026 season. We've seen several cases of deep vein thrombosis in the NBA recently, including with Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama, who missed the final 30 games of the 2024-25 season after doctors discovered deep vein thrombosis in his right shoulder. 
As for superficial thrombophlebitis, Harvard Health Publishing says it can improve over the course of one week to several weeks. However, each case is different. Has this happened before in the NFL?Yes, there are numerous cases of NFL players missing time due to blood clots, and you don't have to look any further than the opponent Philadelphia faces this Sunday. Panthers star right tackle Taylor Moton hasn't played at all this season because doctors found blood clots in his lungs this summer. This was a much more serious situation that required Moton to immediately be placed on blood thinners. Just recently, Moton revealed that he had been off blood thinners for a couple of weeks and could return to the field in the near future. He was listed as a full participant in practice on Wednesday. 
Former first-round pick center Billy Price announced his retirement in 2024 after undergoing emergency surgery for a pulmonary embolism to remove a saddle clot that was entering both of his lungs. He pointed to the risk of internal bleeding while on blood thinners as a reason why he had to hang up the cleats. Kansas City Chiefs Pro Bowl right guard Trey Smith fell to the sixth round of the 2021 NFL Draft despite being a two-time First Team All-SEC player because of concern over blood clots. He was held to just seven games played during his sophomore season at Tennessee after it was discovered that blood clots had returned in his lungs. Smith lost weight, underwent a six-month round of anticoagulants after consulting with specialists, and was eventually cleared to play football again. Smith's history with blood clots was a clear "con" on his scouting report, but he's had zero issues since being selected at No. 226 overall. He is a two-time Super Bowl champion. New Orleans Saints wide receiver Chris Olave and New England Patriots defensive tackle Christian Barmore are two other players who have dealt with blood clots. 
Each situation is different, and most of these situations are different from the one Hurts is currently facing. From what we know at the moment, his clot has thankfully not traveled to his lung.What happens now?Ian Rapoport reported that Hurts cannot play football until this situation is solved. As mentioned above, treatment for blood clots can include blood thinners, and you shouldn't play football on blood thinners. We do not know for a fact that Hurts is going on blood thinners. Other treatments for superficial thrombophlebitis include bed rest, elevating the legs or applying warm compresses, according to Harvard Health Publishing. Every case is different, and it's something that has to be monitored.
How long could Hurts miss?This is a tough question to answer, given that we don't have details on Hurts' clot — other than that it's superficial. We know Hurts will miss Sunday's game vs. Carolina, but Rapoport said the best way to describe his status is "out indefinitely." Eagles' upcoming scheduleWeekOpponent6vs. Carolina Panthers7vs. Dallas Cowboys8at Washington Commanders9vs. New York Giants10BYE

        Awards season has arrived in the WNBA. Ironically, the first two awards announced -- Olivia Miles, Rookie of the Year and Cheryl Reeve, Coach of the Year -- were won by members of the Minnesota Lynx who were eliminated from the playoffs by the New York Liberty, becoming the first No. 1 seed to lose to a No. 8 seed in the first round in WNBA history. Since then, Dallas Wings forward Jessica Shepard (Most Improved Player), Atlanta Dream Angel Reese (Defensive Player of the Year) and Golden State Valkyries forward Janelle Salaün (Sixth Player of the Year) have joined the honorees. As has A'ja Wilson, who won her fifth MVP award and became the first player to win that award in three consecutive seasons. Reeve also added another Executive of the Year award to her trophy case this week and the now-retired Nneka Ogwumike won the Kim Perrot Sportsmanship Award for the fifth time in her career. The All-Rookie Team was highlighted by unanimous Rookie of the Year Olivia Miles and No. 1 overall pick Azzi Fudd, while the All-Defensive Teams were headlined by Wilson and Reese. Still to come are the All-WNBA teams.

    Rookie of the Year: Olivia Miles, LynxMiles, the No. 2 overall pick in the 2026 WNBA Draft, was named the unanimous Rookie of the Year as expected. She is the sixth player to win that honor unanimously, joining Aliyah Boston, A'ja Wilson, Elena Delle Donne, Tina Charles and Candace Parker. 
Miles, who averaged 19.8 points and six assists per game, led all rookies in scoring and assists, and finished eighth and seventh in the league, respectively, in those categories. She also broke Caitlin Clark's rookie points record (790) and led the Lynx to a 33-11 record and the No. 1 seed.

As a full-time starter for the first time in her career, Shepard averaged 14.5 points, 11.1 rebounds and 5.3 assists per game, up from eight points, 7.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists last season. She finished second in the league in rebounding and 11th in assists, was one of two players (along with Angel Reese) to average a double-double, led the league with six triple-doubles and recorded just the second 20-20-10 game in WNBA history. Shepard beat out Shakira Austin and Carla Leite in a close race. Marina Mabrey, Dominique Malonga and Rae Burrell also received votes.

That was thanks in large part to a tremendous coaching performance from Reeve, who helped turn Miles into one of the league's best players and got her new-look group to gel -- at least until the playoffs. Reeve has now won Coach of the Year five times, extending her record and becoming the first coach in major American professional sports to receive the honor five times. Reeve beat out Natalie Nakase and Sydney Johnson. CoachTeamVotesCheryl ReeveLynx40Natalie NakaseValkyries20Sydney JohnsonMystics14

The Frenchwoman led all bench scorers with 12.7 points per game, and shot 39.2% from 3-point range to help the Valkyries win a franchise record 32 games and earn the No. 2 seed. title: Who is Tanner McKee? Eagles QB's college, NFL career and path to replacing Jalen Hurts - CBS Sports
description: The former Stanford quarterback takes over for Jalen Hurts with Philadelphia trying to end a three-game skid and
body:
The former Stanford quarterback takes over for Jalen Hurts with Philadelphia trying to end a three-game skid and remain in the NFC East race
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:32 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The task of breaking a three-game losing streak and keeping the Philadelphia Eagles afloat in the NFC East falls not on Jalen Hurts in Week 6 but rather on Tanner McKee, a fourth-year backup primed for the biggest opportunity of his NFL career. Hurts is out for the matchup against the Carolina Panthers due to a superficial blood clot, which developed after the Week 4 loss to the Los Angeles Rams and moved following last week's trip to London, resulting in his unavailability for Sunday.While the Eagles do have a third option in rookie Cole Payton, the expectation is that McKee will trot out with the offense when they return to Lincoln Financial Field. He served as Hurts' primary backup last year and was the third-stringer in 2024 and made a combined six appearances with two starts.McKee is not entirely unknown in the NFL, considering his pair of previous starts, but this is by far the most prominent role of his career. With so much pressure facing the Eagles in their quest to rebound from a rocky start to the season, McKee will have more eyes on him this weekend than ever before.So who is McKee, really? Here is everything to know about his football career, from his rise as a highly touted high school recruit to his emergence as Philadelphia's Week 6 starter.
Blue-chip recruitMcKee landed on the national radar during his junior year at Corona (Calif.) High School. Centennial. It was the most productive season of his prep career and earned him recognition as a Top247 recruit, and he later climbed as high as No. 38 overall in the 247Sports rankings for the Class of 2018. McKee closed the recruiting cycle as the top four-star quarterback with only three five-star prospects ahead of him: Trevor Lawrence, Justin Fields and JT Daniels.
As a three-sport athlete who also played volleyball and basketball at Centennial, McKee's future was always in football, and he elevated his stock with strong showings on the all-star circuit. He won the MVP award at the 2018 Polynesian Bowl, earned a spot in the U.S. Army All-American Bowl and reached the finals at both The Opening and Elite 11.McKee already held scholarship offers from myriad Power Five schools when Stanford called. Programs across the country sought his talents. Even though Stanford was his ultimate choice and much closer to home than the other programs he was interested in, it was not an open-and-shut case that he would end up with the Cardinal. Stanford was the last school to extend him an offer and the penultimate school to welcome him for an official visit. By the time he took his official visit in January 2018, he had already been on campus for regular-season games at Texas, Texas A&M, Alabama and Washington.
Each of those other schools pushed hard to land him, but come National Signing Day in February 2018, it was Stanford that earned McKee's commitment. The only hiccup for the Cardinal was that its prized signee would not arrive for another two years.The long road to Stanford's lineupAs a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, McKee embarked on a two-year mission in Brazil. The COVID-19 pandemic cut his mission short by about five weeks, and upon his return to the United States, uncertainty about the 2020 college football season left him without a firm answer as to when he would join the Cardinal and eventually suit up as a freshman quarterback. His roster spot was waiting for him, though, and he was physically ready to join the team thanks to a workout regimen he and a fellow missionary adhered to in Brazil."Because we had that weight room in my last area, I think I gained back 10 pounds," McKee said to Deseret News after returning from his mission. "That was super nice. We worked out every morning and I was able to get a little bit back in shape. He threw the rugby ball and I threw the football. Now, when I throw, my arm doesn't really get sore. It's nice to come back home and work out at full speed."
The Pac-12 delayed the start of its season due to the pandemic and was the last of the power conferences to begin play. Stanford held just six games that year, with one against Washington State canceled due to virus protocols. McKee was supposed to be the No. 3 quarterback on Stanford's roster but was elevated to the backup job in the opener when a false positive COVID-19 test kept Davis Mills out of action. That game against No. 12 Oregon got out of hand, and McKee made his lone appearance of the season late in a 35-14 loss.Mills departed for the NFL at the end of that campaign, which sparked a competition between McKee and incumbent backup Jack West for the starting job in 2021. West won the job out of fall camp but lost it when he threw two interceptions in a 24-7 season-opening loss to Kansas State. McKee took over and never looked back.Emergence as NFL prospectThe first start of McKee's college career was an indication of the highlights to come. He orchestrated a 42-28 upset win on the road at No. 14 USC and kept the momentum rolling with two more wins in the next three games, including one over the same Oregon team that defeated the Cardinal the year prior. The Ducks were the No. 3 team in the nation at the time and stood on the wrong end of a breakout performance for McKee in which he racked up 230 yards and three touchdowns in an overtime thriller.
That Oct. 2 victory was the last of Stanford's season, though, as everything went off the rails. McKee missed two games due to injury during a seven-game losing streak to close the year.While the team's overall struggles continued into a three-win 20222 season, McKee did his part as one of the few bright spots on the roster. He started all 12 games and posted a 62% completion rate with 2,947 passing yards and 13 touchdowns to eight interceptions. He also ran for two scores.McKee's performance as a two-year starter made him a draftable quarterback and led him to leave Stanford a year early. He declared for the 2023 NFL Draft and was selected with the 188th overall pick in the sixth round. That marked the start of what is now a four-year tenure with the Eagles.
Career backup with a Super Bowl ringHurts had already established himself as a star quarterback by the time McKee arrived in Philadelphia. He was fresh off the best year of his career: A 2022 campaign in which he earned second-team All-Pro recognition. McKee was never going to be more than a backup, and he spent his rookie year in the No. 3 role behind Hurts and Marcus Mariota. He did not play that season.McKee's first opportunity for playing time came in 2024. With Hurts in concussion protocol and backup Kenny Pickett dealing with an in-game rib injury, McKee was thrust into action in Week 17, and he could not have performed much better as two of his three completions went for touchdowns.
McKee then made his first career start in the regular-season finale and was similarly effective in a 27-for-41, 269-yard, two-touchdown win over the New York Giants. The best part of that season, though? McKee was on the sideline when the Eagles won the Super Bowl.
It was not until Week 18 of the following season that McKee returned to the starting lineup. The Eagles had already locked up their postseason position and rested their starters, and with McKee holding the primary backup job that year, he was the next man up at quarterback. He threw for 241 yards and a touchdown but also logged his first career interception in a loss to the Washington Commanders.First meaningful startWhen McKee leads the Philadelphia offense onto the field on Sunday, it will be his first start outside of Week 18. And depending on the severity of Hurts' blood clot and how long it takes for him to return to the lineup, McKee might be in line to make consecutive starts for the first time. Once Hurts is cleared to play, though, the Eagles will almost certainly thrust him back into action. Even amid a difficult start to the year and even as it seems the Eagles could be trending toward a rebuild, everything is still ahead of them.McKee will have a chance to solidify his job as a No. 2 NFL quarterback against the Panthers, but the chances of a strong performance amounting to much more than that are slim. This is a prime spot for him to shine, considering the Panthers' defense is undermanned and just allowed 32 points in its last outing. Starting cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson are on injured reserve, which opens the door for McKee to pick apart the back end of the Carolina defense. He might have to do it without top wide receiver DeVonta Smith, though, as he continues to nurse a hamstring injury.

        Erin Blanchfield has spent much of her UFC career being told she's a future champion. Five years after her debut, she's still waiting to prove it. Blanchfield can strengthen her case on Saturday against Jasmine Jasudavicius at UFC Fight Night in Edmonton, but winning might not be enough in an increasingly crowded women's flyweight title picture. Blanchfield knows she needs to make a statement.Blanchfield was 22 when she made her UFC debut, quickly establishing herself as one of the division's most promising prospects. She's come close to a title shot before but has never crossed the finish line. Her unanimous decision loss to Manon Fiorot, her only UFC defeat, didn't help, but neither did the circumstances surrounding the championship.The trilogy between Valentina Shevchenko and Alexa Grasso effectively froze the division for nearly two years. Blanchfield found comfort in the delay at that time, reasoning that additional time would only make her better prepared for an eventual title opportunity. These days, it's harder to maintain that perspective. Shevchenko's injury, Natalia Silva's emergence as champion and Grasso's resurgence risk another logjam at the top of the division. Blanchfield, once seemingly destined for a title shot, is again left wondering when her opportunity will come."It's frustrating. I'd be lying if I said it wasn't," Blanchfield told CBS Sports. "If it's not your time, it's not your time. You have to wait and keep working." 
Blanchfield tried to navigate around the delay. When rumors surfaced about Shevchenko's injury, Blanchfield and her manager contacted the UFC, angling to fight for the vacant championship. She was already booked against Jasudavicius, but was ready to abandon those plans for the chance to become champion. The UFC went in another direction, booking Silva against Wang Cong at UFC 332.
"They didn't reach out to me. My manager and I reached out to them because I wanted to put my hat in, if that was an option or opportunity," Blanchfield said. "They wanted Wang Cong to take that fight, and I had my fight already. That definitely sucked a bit in the moment, but I had to quickly say, 'Whatever, that's not happening.' I have this fight. I need to perform, and everything else can come after that." Wang's selection was controversial. She had won several consecutive fights and carried the distinction of having beaten Shevchenko in kickboxing more than a decade ago. However, there were more established contenders ahead of her in the UFC rankings, despite being booked or coming off losses.Blanchfield had an especially difficult time reconciling the decision. Wang earned her title opportunity after defeating Tracy Cortez by decision. Blanchfield had recently finished the same opponent.
"That was the most frustrating part about it, that I had beaten and finished Tracy. Wang beat her by decision and got the title shot," Blanchfield said. "But I really believe God's way is different than our way and what we want. Everything happens for a reason. Everything happens on a certain timeline. That really helped me to focus on my fight, which is literally two weeks after theirs. Time-wise, it lines up for me to win this and potentially get a title shot."Obstacles remain between Blanchfield and the championship. Shevchenko figures to be the first in line for an immediate title shot whenever she's healthy enough to return. The timeline is uncertain, however, and Silva has already identified Blanchfield and Grasso as potential challengers. Blanchfield doesn't have the name recognition of either former champion. She also has the disadvantage of fighting lower-ranked Jasudavicius in her opponent's native Canada, where a routine decision victory will do little to separate her from the other contenders.
"I need an impressive win. An impressive finish. " Blanchfield said. "That's something every fighter is always chasing, especially when you're this close to a title. It's not just about winning, but how you win."Grasso has made a particularly compelling case for another championship opportunity. The former champion has enjoyed a remarkable resurgence this year, brutally finishing Maycee Barber before knocking down and defeating Fiorot. Grasso's latest victory carries particular significance for Blanchfield, whose only UFC loss came against the French contender. Blanchfield isn't pretending Grasso's recent performances have gone unnoticed."She's looked amazing in her last two fights. I don't know what's going on with her personally, but it seems to be headed in the right direction," Blanchfield said. "You can see it in her walkout, how locked in and focused she is. She goes in there, and she really performs to that ability. She's found her second wind, and she looks really good."
Blanchfield can only attempt to control what happens against Jasudavicius. Even an emphatic victory won't guarantee her the next title shot, something she's become painfully familiar with over the years. She viewed the extended Shevchenko-Grasso rivalry as a blessing in disguise. She still believes these extra fights have made her better, even if she's less enthusiastic about having to wait for another opportunity. "I feel like with all these fights that I'm having in the meantime, I've been in title contention for years. They've really honed and sharpened me, and made me a better fighter," Blanchfield said. "It's something I needed even if I didn't want it. "Everybody wants to get to the title as fast as possible. It's a journey to the title. I know it'll be even harder after that because you'll only be fighting the absolute best. I've just been sharpening my tools while I wait."

title: Guess who wins with a 24-team College Football Playoff? Spoiler alert: It's not the fans - CBS Sports
description: Scrapping conference title games and letting four-loss teams crash the field only cheapens the regular season to
body:
Scrapping conference title games and letting four-loss teams crash the field only cheapens the regular season to pacify boosters lighting money on fire
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026

    4:17 pm ET

        Critics have claimed for years that college football would ruin the regular season through endless playoff expansion. It didn't happen with four teams, where the bubble was still quality. The postseason race still mattered with the 12-team field, when quality teams still found themselves on the outside. In reportedly moving to a 24-team playoff, college football has officially jumped the shark. According to reports, the 24-team playoff will lead to the end of conference championship games. The leaders of college football have done almost everything in their power to try and mortgage the soul of the sport for more money in recent years. The 24-team playoff is a massive strike to the heart. For a moment, let's look at what the bubble would have looked like one year ago. The last at-large spot would have gone to 8-4 Iowa. The Hawkeyes went 0-4 against AP Top 25 opponents. The 9-3 Georgia Tech Yellow Jackets actually beat ranked Clemson, but the Tigers finished 7-6. The rest of the bubble included 9-3 Michigan, 8-5 Duke and 8-4 Illinois. 
There's a perception that making the postseason would lead to additional attention and focus on programs that make the playoff. Instead, fans will soon realize that the quality of slop they're being presented will fall precipitously. They'll just be expected to see a mediocre matchup between No. 14 Tennessee and No. 19 USC and keep it moving. Amazingly, there's not even clear evidence that the playoff will even lead to a financial windfall. Conferences will lose tens of millions in rights fees after canceling conference title games, and there's no guarantee they'll make much additional profit. So when it comes down to it… why are we doing this? Unfortunately, the answer is pretty simple. Donors are investing tens of millions of dollars every year into mediocre rosters, and it's time to manufacture a return on investment. 
According to 247Sports, Auburn, Nebraska and Wisconsin are spending more than $30 million on their rosters. Rutgers, South Carolina and Arkansas are spending more than $20 million. None of these schools have a realistic pathway to the College Football Playoff in a 12-team world. In a 24-team world, they still wouldn't get in, but they could at least convince themselves of a path. So really, the playoff is expanding so South Carolina and Maryland can lie to their donors and pretend they're not lighting money on fire. The comprehensive quality of the product on the field is of limited consideration. There's only one problem: Everyone will figure out the grift quickly. Coaches will soon be fired despite making the College Football Playoff, or even after winning first-round games. No fans or donors will be placated by a mediocre team that nominally makes the postseason. Instead, there's a far greater chance that coaches will sign undeserved extensions that lock their fans into misery. 
Individual games, like Notre Dame vs. BYU or Ohio State vs. Indiana this week, lose their luster when they're check-ins with limited stakes. The 12-team playoff manages to create short- and long-term stakes; all are gone in a 24-team playoff for many Power Four teams. And by making the national championship the only marker of success for college football, it ruins much of the fabric that makes college football so special. Winning a conference championship should matter. Beating rivals should matter. It shouldn't just be a massive race for bleeding fans and donors dry. The FCS level at least shows us a model of how a 24-team playoff can make sense. The 11 non-HBCU conferences each receive an auto-bid to the postseason, meaning conference championship races are crucial. It forces a level of breadth across the sport. Of course there's no consideration for the Group of Six at this point. The leaders of the sport only care about hoarding access. 
Making the postseason is supposed to be hard in college football. There are supposed to be consequences for regular season games. But with a 24-team playoff now on the horizon, it's hard not to wonder: What is the point here?

        Penn State and Michigan will meet on Saturday in a matchup between two teams already in desperation mode midway through the season. Both began the 2026 season hopeful for the future with a new coach in charge. Six weeks into the season, that hope and optimism have turned into doom and gloom for both programs that enter Week 7 on losing streaks in Big Ten play. The Wolverines began the season with a controversial win before beating Oklahoma in Week 2 for what seemed, at the time, like Kyle Whittingham's first signature win in Ann Arbor. However, successive losses to Iowa and Minnesota, where the offense has looked inept, have raised the temperature under Whittingham just five games into his tenure. The Nittany Lions had a lengthy coaching search before finally bringing in Matt Campbell from Iowa State, and Penn State fans expected a swift return to Big Ten contention. Three consecutive losses to open conference play have already raised questions about Campbell's fit in State College, and he finds himself in desperation mode heading on the road into a hostile environment. 
For years, Penn State vs. Michigan was one of the biggest games of the year in the old Big Ten East. This year, what it lacks in intrigue regarding the College Football Playoff race, it makes up for in what it will tell us about the trajectory of two traditional Big Ten powers. The winner will be able to let out a sigh of relief, while the loser will be staring down a fight just to make it to a bowl game in 2026.   Michigan vs. Penn State: Need to know  Bryce Underwood as a runner: In Michigan's biggest win of the season against Oklahoma, it was Underwood running the ball that was the difference for the Wolverines. He carried the ball 18 times for 87 yards and one touchdown, which was by far his most productive rushing game of the season. The Penn State defense has struggled this season, and both Aidan Chiles and Colton Joseph have rushed for touchdowns against them for Northwestern and Wisconsin. Throwing the ball consistently hasn't been a strength of the Michigan offense, and in a game they desperately need, look for the Wolverines to try and take advantage of Underwood as a runner at times -- especially in red zone opportunities. Can Penn State create explosive plays?: Moving the ball on Michigan's defense consistently is a difficult task, and in both of their losses, it was explosives that led to scores for Minnesota and Iowa. Penn State's offense ranks in the middle of the pack in explosive plays this season, but has not been as dynamic since Koby Howard's injury took away their top downfield threat. If the Nittany Lions are going to score against Michigan, they have to find a way to produce some explosive plays. That doesn't always have to mean on offense. Iowa's first touchdown against Michigan came on a punt return. Minnesota forced three turnovers that led to 13 of their 20 points. Penn State will need a handful of chunk plays from the offense and to create some havoc on defense and special teams if they're going to win this game. 
Special teams, special teams, special teams: This is the kind of game where special teams matter a bit more than usual -- which is to say, this is going to be Big Ten football heritage on display. The punters on both sides need to be sharp and avoid handing the opponent a short field. With points at a premium, field goal opportunities will need to be converted. And with two offenses that can get stuck in the mud, a big return could swing this game one way or the other. Special teams has not been the strength of the Wolverines this season, as they rank 89th in special teams SP+, while Penn State is in the middle of the pack (49th). The team that wins the special teams battle will gain a considerable advantage, and for underdog Penn State in particular, being sharp in the third phase is a must to win on the road. Where to watch Michigan vs. Penn State live  Date: Saturday, Oct. 17 | Time: 3:30 p.m. ET  Location: Michigan Stadium -- Ann Arbor, MichiganTV: CBS | Live stream: CBSSports.com, CBS Sports App  Streaming on Paramount+ Premium

Michigan games have finished with fewer than 40 total points four times in five games -- with the lone exception being against lowly UTEP -- and even against a leaky Nittany Lions defense, it's hard to see this Michigan offense being overly explosive. body:
Philadelphia needs to remain focused on an NFC East title, explore QB trades and stay on course in 2026

    3:28 pm ET

        The two-time defending NFC East champion Philadelphia Eagles (2-3) will be without face-of-the-franchise quarterback Jalen Hurts for Week 6 against the Carolina Panthers and possibly beyond. Philadelphia announced an ultrasound on Hurts' calf following a flight back from their London game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in Week 5 revealed a superficial blood clot had moved. The Eagles ruled him out and said in a statement they are determining "the appropriate course of treatment" and that Hurts' "health and safety are our highest priority." There's a chance Philadelphia might be without its Super Bowl MVP-winning quarterback for the foreseeable future. Some teams might take that as a sign to trade away pieces at the trade deadline to reload for 2027, but the Eagles can't do that and shouldn't do that. Philadelphia needs to stay the course and fight to compete in 2026. Here is a look at why, how that could look for the Eagles, what QB they could seek via trade and more. Why the Eagles need to stay the courseThe short answer as to why the Eagles need to continue their push to contend in 2026 is that they've invested too much money into their top-end talent. Eagles general manager Howie Roseman made the following significant investments this offseason along the defensive line:
He inked two-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jalen Carter to a four-year, $152 million extension with $106.85 million guaranteed.He extended former first-round pick defensive tackle Jordan Davis on a three-year, $78 million contract with $64.4 million guaranteed.He traded a 2026 third-round pick and a 2027 third-round pick to the Minnesota Vikings for Pro Bowl edge rusher Jonathan Greenard and a 2026 seventh-round pick. Roseman then signed Greenard to a four-year, $98 million extension with $50 million guaranteed. After Hurts' five-year, $255 million contract, these three defensive linemen are the Eagles' next three highest-paid players in terms of total contract value. The Eagles still have one of the more talented rosters in football, especially on defense with those three, former first-round pick edge rusher Nolan Smith Jr., All-Pro linebacker Zack Baun, former first-round pick linebacker Jihaad Campbell, All-Pro cornerback Quinyon Mitchell, All-Pro cornerback Cooper DeJean and Super Bowl champion cornerback Riq Woolen. Even though former NFL Offensive Player of the Year running back Saquon Barkley (hamstring) and wide receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring/toe) are battling injuries, they're two high-level playmakers when on the field. This defense is talented enough to keep the Eagles in almost every game. Yes, it's felt like the sky is falling after consecutive losses to the Los Angeles Rams and the Jaguars, in which they blew the lead in the final two minutes. There's a world where they're just a couple plays away from being 4-1 instead of 2-3. NFC East still up for grabsThis isn't a situation like the Kansas City Chiefs in 2025, who went 6-11 amid an up-and-down year that saw quarterback Patrick Mahomes go down with a torn ACL. The 2026 Eagles are a much more talented roster than those Chiefs, and their division is much, much worse. 
Last season, the AFC West division champion Denver Broncos were the AFC's No. 1 seed with a 14-3 record. The Los Angeles Chargers gutted out an 11-6 Wild Card campaign with quarterback Justin Herbert playing the role of miracle worker behind a battered offensive line. This season, no one seems to want to win the NFC East. Week 5 was a prime example of that. The Dallas Cowboys (2-3) lost 24-16 at home on "Thursday Night Football" to the previously winless Tampa Bay Buccaneers, with Jalon Daniels, an undrafted rookie quarterback, making his second career start. Dallas has the NFL's 31st-ranked total defense (395.4 total yards per game allowed), last-place run defense (168.4 rushing yards per game allowed), and last-place third-down defense (52.6% third-down conversion rate allowed). If Daniels can march up and down the field on the Cowboys, so can Philadelphia.The Eagles had the least embarrassing loss of the week, a 19-17 defeat against the AFC South-leading Jaguars despite kicking a go-ahead field goal with eight seconds left. People fault coach Nick Sirianni for having the kickoff go in bounds to drain time off the clock. The Jaguars returned the kick 53 yards to the Eagles' 39, which set up the game-winning, 57-yard field goal for Jacksonville. 
The NFC East-leading New York Giants (3-1-1) tied 27-27 against the last-place Washington Commanders (1-3-1) even though both teams reached field-goal range in the last two minutes of overtime. New York is without quarterback Jaxson Dart and All-Pro edge rusher Brian Burns for the year because of season-ending knee injuries. A path toward a third straight division title and a home playoff game in the opening round of the postseason is still well within reach. Sirianni's standard is too high, and he needs to show he can adapt the offenseSirianni's 67-33 career record, including the playoffs, is tied for the fifth-best record in the first 100 games by an NFL head coach since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger, per CBS Sports Research. Philadelphia has made the playoffs every year under his watch, including winning the NFC twice and winning Super Bowl LIX. 
After the current three-game losing streak the Eagles are on, which began with a lifeless "Monday Night Football" defeat to the Case Keenum-led Chicago Bears, Sirianni is under fire. His background is on the offensive side of the ball, but the Eagles are bottom 10 in the entire league in the following metrics: scoring offense (18.4 points per game, 29th), total offense (262.2 total yards per game, 31st) and rushing offense (91.6, tied for 23rd).The problem appears to be that Sirianni isn't letting new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion fully implement his scheme. Mannion came to Philadelphia after spending last season as the Green Bay Packers quarterbacks coach under Matt LaFleur. He also played for Sean McVay and the Rams and Kevin O'Connell and the Minnesota Vikings across his nine-season playing career. Mannion is a branch off the Shanahan-McVay coaching tree, which tends to have offenses that display heavy doses of motion, quarterbacks lining up under center and play-action passing. The scheme wants the looks for runs and passes to appear the same to defenses. That way, the quarterback should be able to easily run a given play as called and then take advantage of a defense that can't tell what's coming. 
In Mannion's offense under Sirianni, the Eagles are just average in motion rate (57.8%, 13th in the NFL) while ranking bottom-five in under-center rate (31.1%, 28th) and dead last in play-action rate (16.7%). Running the Shanahan-McVay offense without its core staples is like trying to play video games without plugging the console's HDMI cord into the TV: It's not going to work. As odd as it may sound, losing Hurts and having a three-game losing streak (tied for the longest under Sirianni), may create the desperation necessary for Sirianni to let Mannion open up his entire playbook. Eagles should peruse the QB trade market and/or ride with Tanner McKeeIt certainly makes sense for Roseman to pick up the phone and call around the league to see what top-flight backup quarterbacks are up for grabs. The problem is that many of the NFL's more experienced backup quarterbacks play for fellow NFC contenders. 
The 5-0 San Francisco 49ers likely won't trade Mac Jones to the Eagles. The same goes for the 5-0 Minnesota Vikings and former Philadelphia starter Carson Wentz, and the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks (3-2) aren't shipping Drew Lock out east either. No way the Green Bay Packers (3-2) part with Tyrod Taylor to help out Philadelphia. A realistic one-season target could be Cincinnati Bengals backup quarterback Joe Flacco, an alum of Audubon High School just over seven miles down the road from Lincoln Financial Field (the home of the Eagles). Flacco is 41 years old, but the ex-Super Bowl MVP proved he can be a steady stand-in when needed. He exploded for 342 yards passing and three touchdowns on 31-of-47 passing in a 33-31 "Thursday Night Football" victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 7 last season. He followed up that effort by going toe-to-toe with Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears in Week 9, throwing for a career-high 470 yards, four passing touchdowns and two interceptions in a narrow defeat. He is very comfortable simply getting the ball to his playmakers and letting them do the rest at this age.If Cincinnati won't part with its Joe Burrow injury insurance plan, then it's worth seeing what backup quarterback Tanner McKee can do. The 26-year-old sixth-round pick from the 2023 NFL Draft was a four-star recruit coming out of high school before a mission trip paused his football career for two years. 
McKee only has two career starts, both in Week 18 of the last two seasons. At the end of the 2024 regular season, he completed 27 of his 41 throws for 269 yards and two touchdowns in a 20-13 win over the New York Giants. Last season, he struggled against Washington, completing just 21 of 40 throws for 241 yards, a touchdown and an interception in a 24-17 defeat.With McKee, Flacco, or potentially another veteran at quarterback, the Eagles have enough high-end, highly-paid talent — along with sky-high expectations — for Philadelphia to continue its pursuit of a third straight NFC East division title. The rest of the division is practically daring the Eagles to come seize their crown. Whenever Hurts can return is a scenario to address when the team has more information. Until then, Philadelphia should remain full steam ahead in 2026.

title: NBA's most overrated players: James Harden and Paul George make list -- and so do some young All-Stars - CBS Sports
description: Who are the most overrated players in the NBA as a new season begins? Here's what our staff thinks
body:
Who are the most overrated players in the NBA as a new season begins? Here's what our staff thinks
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                            
        
    Oct 15, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:52 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            7 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Earlier this week we published our CBS Sports Top 100 NBA player rankings, knowing it's impossible for anyone to agree on these sorts of lists. That's sort of the point of doing them. They're (hopefully civil) conversation starters. One person might have Victor Wembanyama as the No. 1 player heading into the 2026-27 season, another person may have Nikola Jokić or Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, but everyone is going to have those guys near the top of their list. For the purposes of this article you're about to read, we're looking for the significant discrepancies between where a player ranked on the CBS Sports final list, which was a creation of cumulative staff votes, and where a player ranked on our individual list. Based on these discrepancies, we published our most underrated players on Wednesday (James Harden was one of them), and now we're polling our writers for their most overrated players (James Harden is again one of them). See, reasonable minds can disagree. Let's get to it.  Evan Mobley, Cavaliers 
Top 100 ranking: 22 Why that's too high: Mobley is clearly talented and a phenomenal defender, but I have a hard time buying a guy who is a third option offensively as the 22nd best player in the league. Mobley took a step back as a shooter last year and given he's also not a dominant interior player, there are just a few too many limitations to his offensive game for me to place him as high as some of my colleagues. The defense is fantastic, and he's a productive offensive player, but I am in the "need to see it to believe it" camp with regards to another leap coming from him that puts him into that top-20 conversation. -- Robby Kalland 
        
            
                Ranking the NBA's top 100 players: Victor Wembanyama enters 2026-27 season at No. 1
                
                    Sam Quinn                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
 Jalen Duren, Pistons 
Top 100 ranking: No. 34 Why that's too high: In an alternate universe, Duren might land on the underrated list. He bet on himself last year and made his first All-Star and All-NBA teams. Then he went out and faceplanted in the postseason, getting badly outplayed by Wendell Carter Jr. for much of the first round against the Magic and then mostly being a no-show against the Cavs in the second round. When Cade Cunningham desperately needed support, Duren's points per game plummeted from 19.5 in the regular season to 10.2 in the playoffs. That decidedly poor performance led to a contentious and protracted contract negotiation between Duren and the Pistons this offseason. Duren eventually signed a new five-year deal worth $200 million, a handsome sum to be sure. But it was also a far cry from the $287 million max contract for which he was eligible. When your own team is playing hardball with you at the bargaining table and there are reports you might rather play for the Kings because you feel "disrespected," maybe something has gone sideways -- sort of like us ranking him ahead of better bigs such as JJJ, Joel Embiid and Anthony Davis. -- John Gonzalez  
 James Harden, Cavaliers 
Top 100 ranking: No. 47 Why that's too high: This is not a career-achievement ranking. When we put this list together, nobody factored in Harden's MVP almost a decade ago or his pre-pandemic scoring title, or at least they shouldn't have. This is a 2026-27 projection. As Brad Pitt said to the dude playing David Justice in Moneyball, "I'm not paying you for the player you used to be, I'm paying you for the player you are right now." And right now Harden is merely a good regular-season player durability and ball-dominant numbers have deceived the Cavs into thinking he's worth $100 million over the next three years (well, that and they traded Darius Garland, who's 10 years younger and generally the same player, to get him). But I'll tell you what: If we do want to make this a career-based evaluation, how about those 48 career playoff games that Harden has had more turnovers than shots made? Forty-eight! He had seven of them in last year's postseason, when he averaged 19 points and five assists on 29% 3-point shooting. Do you have any idea how many NBA players could average pretty damn close to those numbers if their team gave them the ball as often as Harden? A lot. Those are not even close to good enough numbers from a guy who has to be extraordinarily good offensively to cover for his continued pathetic defense. At the end of the day, Harden is an innings eater. He's going to get you through the 82-game slog, but you do not want him on the mound in the playoffs. I'm just going to go down the list of guys ranked behind him in our Top 100 and name the guys I am very confident most coaches/GMs would prefer to have on their team over Harden through the lens of winning playoff basketball: Jaden McDaniels, Trey Murphy III, Mikal Bridges, Desmond Bane, Damian Lillard, Josh Hart, Aaron Gordon, Alex Caruso, Payton Pritchard, Jrue Holiday, RJ Barrett, Devin Vassell, Ajay Mitchell, and I'm leaving guys like Cason Wallace and Isaiah Hartenstein and Draymond Green off because I know people who only know how to look at box scores are going to laugh at that. But trust me, if a GM would rather have Harden running their team than Draymond, even at this point in his career, playing his role going into a playoff game, they either don't know ball or secretly want to get fired. 
I know the argument against some of these guys I just named is that they can't be the focal point of an offense, but listen, if you're a real playoff team, you already have that guy, and he's much better than Harden. For the Cavs, that's Donovan Mitchell. Winning playoff games becomes about having as many winning support players around the star(s) as possible. The Cavs would be a bigger threat in the playoffs with any one of the guys I just listed than Harden. They just don't have the name value. -- Brad Botkin  Paul George, Celtics 
Top 100 ranking: No. 67 Why that's too high: Even though the trade happened over three months ago, I'm still trying to wrap my head around the Celtics willingly trading their second-best player (Jaylen Brown), who is also a consensus top-20 player around the league, for … Paul George? It would've been a great trade maybe seven years ago, when George was coming off an MVP-finalist season with Oklahoma City, but not only has George declined as a player, but he also has one of the worst contracts in the league. The Celtics are one of the smartest organizations in sports, so I still can't wrap my head around the trade. But going back to George's ranking, I think it's about 20 spots too high. George is still a good player, but I would comfortably take 15-20 players over him in our top 100 right now. Maybe he proves me wrong and has a great season with Boston, but I was surprised to see names like Cason Wallace, Domantas Sabonis, Ivica Zubac, RJ Barrett, Ajay Mitchell and even Ja Morant ranked behind him. -- Cameron Salerno 
 Brandon Ingram, Clippers 
Top 100 ranking: No. 76 Why that's too high: I've never been able to get over Brandon Ingram's 3-point volume miraculously rising during contract years and then regressing back to the norm after he's signed. Maybe it's a coincidence, but it feels as though Ingram struggles to find the balance between the shot diet the NBA likely wants for him and the mid-range heavy approach he seems to prefer. There are elements of this dilemma throughout Ingram's game. At points, he's shown basically every skill you'd want a high-end wing to have. He defended really well at the end of his Lakers tenure, and it didn't follow him to New Orleans. He'll have stretches as a legitimate playmaking plus and then they'll disappear thereafter. All of it folds together into a player that can frustratingly feel like less than the sum of his parts. We don't know when exactly he suffered that partially torn Achilles and how much it affected him in the playoffs... but it feels notable that Toronto was substantially more competitive against Cleveland without its second All-Star than with him last spring. Scoring was a chore without Ingram in that series ... but it was a chore with him as well, and the younger Raptors gave Cleveland a series by mucking up the game and defending extremely well. The skill has always been here for Ingram. It just never adds up into the sort of impact on winning that you'd hope for. -- Sam Quinn

        Jeff Lebby knows Lane Kiffin better than most. Lebby ran Kiffin's offense at Ole Miss in 2020 and 2021, and the Rebels' 2020 attack set an SEC record for total offense in conference play. Kiffin called him "a huge part of our success there" this week. Now Mississippi State's head coach, he leads the Bulldogs into a top-25 showdown with LSU on Saturday."I don't like playing against him because they go so fast," Kiffin said this week.LSU (4-2, 1-2 SEC) is reeling after an overtime loss at Kentucky last week, and finds itself in a familiar place under previous coaches: two losses at the midpoint of the season. It wasn't supposed to start this way for Kiffin, who took over a program with deep pockets and turned the roster over into one of the most talented in the country. A third conference loss in Kiffin's first season would leave almost no margin for November, with Alabama and Texas still coming to Baton Rouge.
Mississippi State (4-1, 2-1) has already won two SEC games, exceeding the one Lebby collected in his first two seasons combined. Alabama rode into Starkville and won 56-23 two weeks ago, and Kamario Taylor, the sophomore quarterback who spent September in the Heisman Trophy conversation, finished the day on the sideline with a boot on his right foot.Two weeks later, nobody outside the Bulldogs' building knows if he will play. Lebby said the SEC availability report would answer that question. LSU vs. Mississippi State: Need to knowKamario Taylor's right foot: Taylor has thrown for 1,450 yards and an SEC-best 17 touchdowns with four interceptions. He's thrown three touchdowns in the last five games, the longest stretch since LSU's Jayden Daniels in 2023. He first hurt his foot in the win over Missouri, and it showed against the Tide. He was sacked five times and finished with minus-26 rushing yards before leaving the game. If he can't play, Lebby's options are redshirt freshman Parker Puckett and AJ Swann, who spent a season at LSU. 
Where is Mississippi State's ground game? Fluff Bothwell has 403 yards and three touchdowns on 74 carries, but he had only one carry against Alabama and spent most of the afternoon with a boot on his left foot. The Bulldogs were outrushed 179-18. Now they get a defense that ranked second nationally against the run through four weeks, allowing 47.5 yards per game. Kentucky found cracks last week. CJ Baxter broke a 77-yard run on the first snap and finished with 123 yards. The Wildcats ran for 155 yards.The Sam Leavitt Experience: LSU QB Sam Leavitt has thrown for 1,496 yards and 10 touchdowns, but he has thrown an interception in every game this season, totaling eight through six games. No one in the FBS has thrown more interceptions. At Kentucky, he completed 25 of 34 passes for 275 yards and two touchdowns and ran for another in overtime, but he also threw a pick and lost a fumble on a sack in the fourth quarter. LSU's recent success: The Tigers have won the last three meetings against Mississippi State. The Bulldogs last won in Baton Rouge in 2020, when they pulled off a 44-34 upset in Mike Leach's first season. This is the first meeting since 2023. The teams used to play each other annually, but that ended when the SEC expanded to 16 teams in 2024.

Not one cleared 58.5. Kiffin's offense averages 42 points per game, but against SEC defenses LSU has scored 24, 35 and 27 in regulation.
Mississippi State scores 39 points per game, but that production was built on Taylor's legs and Bothwell's workload. Both are in question against a front that has been among the nation's best against the run. Mississippi State's SEC games have averaged nearly 70 total points, and if Taylor is close to 100%, Lebby's tempo can drag LSU into a bayou shootout. The Crimson Tide will be looking to avoid losing consecutive regular season games for the first time since 2007, while the Volunteers will be seeking to snap a four-game home losing streak against ranked opponents.Alabama (5-1, 3-1 SEC) took a 20-17 home loss to Georgia last week, which leaves the Crimson Tide with a dwindling margin for error entering the second half of their schedule. Tennessee (5-1, 2-1) is coming off an ugly 24-17 win at Arkansas in need of the resume boost that would come with knocking off Alabama.While Tennessee's defense is thriving midway through the season, facing Alabama will be its toughest test yet. Crimson Tide quarterback Keelon Russell leads the league in passing yards with 1,599 and brings game-changing mobility. Though Alabama star receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams is expected to miss the game due to injury, Bama's offense will still pack a punch that tests Tennessee's secondary.The Volunteers counter with the nation's No. 15 rushing offense and a languishing passing attack that will need to get better if they are going to pull an upset that would reverberate through the SEC and beyond. With blowout road wins over quality foes Kentucky and Mississippi State already in hand, the Tide will look to keep rolling on the road with their first win in Knoxville since 2020.
  Alabama vs. Tennessee: Need to know  Neyland blues: The last time Tennessee beat a ranked team at Neyland Stadium was in 2024, when it edged No. 7 Alabama 24-17. The Vols finished 0-3 at home against ranked opponents last season and fell 20-17 to Texas in Week 4, extending their home losing streak against ranked opponents to four games. But something will have to give as the Crimson Tide have dropped two straight inside Neyland Stadium. Whichever team is smoking, the traditional postgame victory cigars will hit a little different this time.Tennessee's QB question: Tennessee sophomore quarterback George MacIntyre made his first career start last week in the Volunteers' 24-17 win at Arkansas, stepping in for injured and underperforming freshman Faizon Brandon. Now the question is how long the Volunteers will stick with MacIntyre, who completed 18 of 29 passes for 247 yards with a touchdown and two interceptions against the Razorbacks. Regardless of who gets the nod against Alabama, the Crimson Tide's priority will be to slow down the SEC's second-leading rusher, DeSean Bishop, and to make Tennessee's fledgling passing attack prove that it can deliver.Playoff implications: With a win, Alabama will have an 87.7% chance of reaching the College Football Playoff, according to the CBS Sports College Football Playoff Forecaster. A loss would drop that mark to 52.9% and crush Alabama's margin for error. Because the Crimson Tide's strength of schedule lags behind others in the SEC, its case for inclusion as a three-loss team would be shaky. Tennessee's playoff odds would shoot to 51.6% with a win and drop to 16.8% with a loss.

Replicating that formula against Alabama won't be possible unless the Crimson Tide shoot themselves in the foot with turnovers and special team miscues. Because the Crimson Tide won't respect the Volunteers' passing game, they'll be able to load the box and frustrate Tennessee's ground game, much like Texas did in Week 4. No. 4 Ohio State is looking for revenge against No. 5 Indiana after last year's Big Ten title game

    4:24 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The 100th all-time meeting between Ohio State and Indiana should be a good one. The fifth-ranked Hoosiers host the fourth-ranked Buckeys with their undefeated record on the line. The winner will have the inside track to Indianapolis.The reigning national champion, Indiana, hasn't faced a single ranked team, and it's had one of the easier schedules in the Big Ten. The Hoosiers did get a dicey road test against Nebraska last weekend, but that was a nice warmup for what's to come on Saturday. Despite losing a number of key pieces from last year's team, Indiana still looks like a serious title contender thanks to newcomers Nick Marsh (528 receiving yards and six touchdowns), Turbo Richard (leads Big Ten in rushing yards) and Tobi Osunsanmi (leads the Big Ten in sacks and tackles for loss).Ohio State will be looking for a little revenge after losing to Indiana in the 2025 Big Ten Championship. That loss snapped the Buckeyes' 30-game winning streak over the Hoosiers, so they'll try to start a new one on Saturday. That's entirely possible, largely due to the presence of Heisman Trophy favorite and athletic anomaly Jeremiah Smith, who leads the conference in just about every major receiving category.This is one of the best games on a loaded Week 7 slate, so here is everything you must know as No. 5 Indiana visits No. 4 Ohio State.
Ohio State vs. Indiana: Need to knowAnnual top-five matchup: For the first 97 meetings between these teams, there were zero top-five matchups. When the game kicks off Saturday, it will be the third time in as many years that Indiana and Ohio State have played with both teams ranked inside the top five. If we're honest, Indiana was the main reason there were no top-five matchups in the first 97 meetings, but that has changed in a big way now. The Hoosiers have the resources and the coach to compete with the Buckeyes, so we may have a budding Big Ten rivalry on our hands.Smith's historic season: Every week, Smith rewrites the record books at the program, conference and NCAA level. That could continue on Saturday because Smith is just one receiving touchdown shy of matching Michigan legend Braylon Edwards for the most in Big Ten history (39). Smith has already secured the school records for career receptions (211), receiving yards (3,474) and receiving touchdowns (38). He should only add to those totals against a Hoosiers secondary Smith beat for 144 yards last year.Sacking Sayin: One way to make sure Smith never gets the football is to hit Ohio State quarterback Julian Sayin while he still has the ball. That's exactly what the Hoosiers did in the Big Ten title game, sacking Sayin five times. Indiana has the personnel to get after Sayin again this time around. Osunsanmi and Stephen Daley have combined for 10 sacks, and Ohio State has allowed 11 sacks of Sayin thus far. The battle between the Indiana defensive front and the Ohio State offensive line in pass protection will be critical.

Having said that, I do wonder how well Indiana's passing defense will hold up for 60 minutes, especially without D'Angelo Ponds in the secondary this time. Ohio State hits enough big plays with Smith to create some breathing room late. Pick: Ohio State -3.5

Texas looks to avenge a loss at Florida that ultimately kept the Longhorns out of the College Football Playoff last season

        Texas coach Steve Sarkisian is sticking to his guns — in this case, his play-calling — and believes the scrutiny of Arch Manning is unjustified heading into Saturday's game against Florida. Manning's inconsistency has kept the Longhorns' offense largely out of rhythm this season, a critique he'll try to correct against the SEC's worst defense. After a loss to rival Oklahoma sent the Longhorns falling six spots in the AP Poll, Texas is hoping to use the tailspinning Gators as their punching bag to stay in the College Football Playoff picture. Florida has lost back-to-back SEC games in blowout fashion, tumbling out of the national rankings without a clear solution to stop the hemorrhaging. Sumrall said progress is sometimes "dysfunctional" and agreed with some of the booing he experienced on the sideline of last week's loss to South Carolina. The Gators struggled to block Gamecocks edge Dylan Stewart and now must endure the athleticism of Colin Simmons, who leads college football with 9.5 sacks. Simmons collected five sacks during a win at Tennessee last month and is the runaway favorite to win the SEC's Defensive Player of the Year honor.
  Texas vs. Florida: Need to know  Turnovers and touchdowns: Manning's production against Power Four competition has been pedestrian -- four touchdown passes and four interceptions. Two came during the fourth quarter of last week's loss to Oklahoma, including a pick-six that swung the game's momentum to the Sooners. Manning's been sacked 12 times through five games -- 10 coming against Ohio State, Tennessee and Oklahoma. If there's a get-right opportunity for Florida's defense, perhaps this is it.Frightening defensive numbers: Florida ranks last in the SEC in total defense, explosive plays allowed, pass defense and 15th in scoring defense this season. Sumrall said this week he was taking a closer look at multiple areas of his team to try and fix what has nuked this 4-0 start for the Gators. It starts with getting stops on defense against the Longhorns.Longhorns' second 'revenge' game: A failure-to-show loss against the Gators in Gainesville ultimately kept Texas out of the CFP last year. Now, Sarkisian's squad has a chance to move to 2-0 this season in revenge opportunities after beating Ohio State in Week 2. Texas remains in this week's updated CFP projection with a first-round home game and has a clear-cut path to the 12-team bracket, but Saturday's a must-win.
Where to watch Texas vs. Florida live  Date: Saturday, Oct. 17 | Time: 12 p.m. ET  Location: Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium -- Austin, TexasTV: ABC | Live stream: Fubo  Texas vs. Florida prediction, picks  Texas has problems on offense, but Florida's even worse on defense. Consecutive SEC blowouts have erased the goodwill from a 4-0 start and No. 8 ranking, and a secondary LaNorris Sellers picked apart last week now gets Manning. Consistency hasn't been Manning's calling card, but this matchup should restore some confidence in the Longhorns' passing game. Florida isn't giving anyone reason to trust its defense, especially against an opponent with something to prove. Last season's loss to the Gators should have Texas' attention. The Longhorns return the favor this weekend. Pick: Texas -10.5
